title: The Madness of Therapy Culture
author: Ashley Frawley
content:
![The Madness of Therapy
Culture](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/Screenshot-2026-11-09-at-8.02.56
---PM.png)

> _All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to
> be Disordered_  
>  By Fredrik DeBoer  
> Simon & Schuster, 336 pages, $30  
>  
>  _Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering_  
>  By Catherine Liu  
> Verso, 192 pages, $24.95

More than a decade ago, I noticed that the walls at the university where I
taught were plastered with posters designed to raise "awareness" about mental
health. When students began to tell me that they were passionate about mental
health, I began to suspect that the word was taking on new meanings. But it
wasn't until one passed me a leaflet in the foyer unhelpfully informing me
that one in four people suffer from "mental health" that I understood what was
happening. Somewhere along the way, the boundaries between mental health and
mental illness had become blurred until the former meant the latter.

Two new books, Fredrik deBoer's _All in Your Head_ and Catherine Liu's
_Traumatized_ , draw attention to one of the strangest achievements of
contemporary therapy culture. Even as psychological suffering has become more
visible, it has become increasingly difficult to speak bluntly about its
degrees, causes, and uneven spread. Everything becomes curiously melded
together and flattened out. Hence, when the British royals set out some years
ago to[ _inform_](https://www.standard.co.uk/news/uk/royals-launch-marathon-
effort-to-end-stigma-about-mental-health-a3365256.html?ref=compactmag.com)
everyone that "we all have mental health," no one should have mistaken what
that[ _meant_](https://people.com/royals/we-all-struggle-with-mental-health-
at-times-says-prince-william/?ref=compactmag.com). Mental health is a
continuum or spectrum, we are often told, and somewhere along it sit students
with exam stress and people convinced their neighbors are poisoning their
water. Everyone is in some sense ill.

Well, not everyone. Even as we are all being told we belong somewhere on the
"mental health" spectrum, the World Health Organization is[
_calling_](https://www.who.int/news/item/09-10-2023-who-ohchr-launch-new-
guidance-to-improve-laws-addressing-human-rights-abuses-in-mental-health-
care?ref=compactmag.com) for an end to "coercive practices in mental health."
The UN Disability Committee is[
_urging_](https://docstore.ohchr.org/SelfServices/FilesHandler.ashx?enc=FnTzN9DhC997%2BytRGB9CiAXgnJCl%2FR7hmmsqdi%2BHFkCUykQENCM8Wf%2BYusFM%2BlimH%2FRpDhdncamxegN8u4umag%3D%3D&ref=compactmag.com)
states to pursue "the abolition of substitute decision-making regimes" in
favor of "supported" alternatives for those we once called "mentally ill," but
who are now variously "people with mental health conditions" or "psychosocial
disabilities." These are people whose suffering often expressly means they are
unable to make decisions for themselves. The rest of us are presumed fragile,
but the psychotic is increasingly presumed sovereign. As deBoer writes, it has
become "our transcendent obligation to pretend that a man in the grip of
psychosis [is] somehow still free."

DeBoer and Liu both show that attempts to flatten out the experience of
suffering, disability, and mental illness fail to accomplish their purported
aims, such as "destigmatizing" and expanding access to care. This is because
reality, whether in the form of the severity of impairment or of social class,
eventually asserts itself, with the consequences falling on those least able
to bear them.
